title: Arvind Raman Steps In as Interim US AI Safety Chief After Chris Fall's Exit
excerpt: The Indian American NIST director will temporarily lead the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, marking the third leadership change at the federal AI testing body in four months.
body:
• Chris Fall resigned as director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) just three months after his appointment, with no reason given by the Commerce Department.
  • NIST Director Arvind Raman, an IIT Delhi alumnus and former Purdue University engineering dean, will lead CAISI on an interim basis.
  • CAISI works with Anthropic, Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Microsoft, and xAI to test unreleased AI models for security vulnerabilities.
  • Fall's departure marks the third leadership change at the agency since early 2026, reflecting ongoing turbulence in the Trump administration's AI policy.

Arvind Raman, the Indian American director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, will temporarily take charge of the federal government's AI testing institute after its director Chris Fall resigned, a Commerce Department spokesperson told Reuters on Sunday.

Fall stepped down just three months after being appointed to lead the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), the federal body responsible for evaluating frontier AI models developed by companies including Anthropic, Google's DeepMind, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Elon Musk's xAI. The Commerce Department did not provide a reason for his departure.

A Revolving Door at America's AI Testing Lab

Fall's exit is the latest in a series of rapid leadership changes at the institute. In April, Collin Burns — a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher — was initially tapped to lead CAISI but was replaced before he could start after the White House realized his previous ties to Anthropic, a company locked in a legal battle with the administration over military use of its AI models.

His swift departure raises fresh questions about the stability of the administration's AI oversight apparatus.

"Dr. Fall brings the scientific leadership needed to ensure America leads the world in evaluating frontier AI models and advancing the technical standards that protect our national and economic security."

— Commerce Department spokesperson, announcing Fall's appointment in April

A spokesperson for President Trump declined to comment on the resignation. Reuters could not immediately reach Fall.

Who Is Arvind Raman?

Raman was sworn in as the 18th NIST director and Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology on June 30, 2026, after being confirmed by the U.S. Senate on May 18. As head of the Commerce Department office that oversees CAISI, he is the natural interim choice.

Born in India, Raman earned a bachelor of technology degree from the Indian Institute of Technology in Delhi before completing his master's at Purdue University and a Ph.D. in mechanical engineering at the University of California, Berkeley. He joined Purdue's faculty in 2000 and rose to become the John A. Edwardson Dean of Engineering in 2023, a role in which the university's engineering program climbed to the top four nationally in U.S. News research rankings.

"I am honored to be nominated to this position by President Trump and Secretary Lutnick, and I look forward to maximizing NIST's ability to accelerate American innovation through partnerships with industry, entrepreneurs and other stakeholders."

— Arvind Raman, upon his swearing-in as NIST director

His research background spans atomic force microscopy, human biomechanics, and electronics manufacturing, with longstanding collaborations with NIST researchers in nanotechnology. He has received a National Science Foundation CAREER award, the Gustus Larson Memorial Award from the American Society of Mechanical Engineers, and a Keeley Fellowship from the University of Oxford.

Trump's Shifting AI Stance

The leadership churn at CAISI mirrors broader uncertainty in the administration's approach to artificial intelligence. Upon returning to office in January 2025, Trump revoked former President Biden's executive order on AI safety and signaled a hands-off approach to the tech sector. But the administration has since taken a more active role in monitoring the technology.

CAISI — formerly known as the AI Safety Institute before being rebranded by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to emphasize "standards" over "safety" — is staffed by scientists and engineers who test unreleased AI models for vulnerabilities. Their focus includes preventing U.S. adversaries from exploiting AI to develop chemical or biological weapons or corrupt the data used to train American AI models.

During his Senate confirmation hearing, Raman pledged to deliver on the president's AI Action Plan while reorienting NIST to its "apolitical mission." He told lawmakers that American leadership in setting global technology standards ensures that "international rules of commerce are literally being based on American values — free markets, private sector innovation, privacy, freedom of speech," according to IndiaWest.

An Indian American at the Helm

Raman's appointment adds to a growing list of Indian Americans in senior U.S. government science and technology roles. His trajectory — from IIT Delhi to the directorship of one of America's oldest and most influential standards bodies — now places him at the center of the country's AI governance debate at a particularly volatile moment.

Whether the role remains interim or evolves into something more permanent will depend on the administration's next move. For now, Raman inherits a testing institute that has seen three directors in roughly four months, with no public explanation for the latest vacancy.
